messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Judge
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Anniversaries: The anniversary of the event, Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event, Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Marisol Bennett, a 52-year-old divorced judge of North American background, had built a life around composure, precision, and being visibly unshaken. Long before she came to court in a dark robe and took her seat above the bench, she had spent several months as a relief worker in a war zone, moving through damaged streets and crowded makeshift shelters where danger felt immediate and ordinary. The event that later came to define her began on an afternoon when she was working among civilians and was suddenly caught in the chaos of armed men in military and police uniforms moving through the area. The uniforms, which she had once associated with order, became part of what she experienced as terrifying and uncontrollable. In the midst of that scene, a particular taste from what she had been given or had tasted during those hours lodged in her memory so strongly that, years later, it could return her to that setting with startling force. What Marisol remembers most is not a detached account but the felt reality of it: the sound of voices and commands, the sensation that everything around her had become unbearable, and the conviction that she was in immediate danger.

After she returned to the United States, Marisol found that the memory did not stay in the past in the way she expected. When it came to mind, she sometimes heard the sounds from that frightening time play in her head as if they were still happening nearby. At those moments, remembering did not feel like recalling a story; it brought back the same terror she had felt then, and at times the memory arrived as though the whole scene were happening again in the present across sight, sound, smell, and bodily sensation all at once. She became especially unsettled by military or police uniforms in ordinary life. A uniformed officer in a courthouse hallway, or a police presence outside the building, could catch her attention so sharply that she would feel her body tighten before she had fully registered what she was seeing. The anniversary of the event was another difficult time. Without planning to, she found herself noticing the date as it approached, bracing for a heaviness she could not fully explain to colleagues. Even a particular taste, something small and ordinary in another setting, could pull her abruptly back to the war zone and make the past feel immediate again.

Over the years, Marisol developed habits aimed at keeping the memories and feelings at bay. She worked hard not to think about the trauma, pushing away thoughts when they surfaced and redirecting herself with the same discipline she used in court. She also avoided circumstances that reminded her of the event, especially being in the dark. After hours in the courthouse, she would prefer bright, familiar spaces and would arrange her evenings to minimize the chance of finding herself in dimly lit places where she felt too exposed to what her mind might bring back. She told herself that maintaining control was necessary and tried hard to manage her emotions so that nothing would spill into her work or show on her face. That effort fit with the role she had built for herself, but it also left her vigilant about how much of herself might be visible to others. Marisol had come to believe that people could see what had happened to her just by looking at her, as if some trace of the war zone remained readable on her body. That sense of being exposed made her feel isolated and set apart, even in rooms full of colleagues and attorneys. She did not say this dramatically; rather, she carried it as a private certainty that separated her from the ordinary flow of conversation and professional life.

Marisol’s daily work as a judge required constant public presence, but it also brought the very kinds of reminders she tried to keep out of reach. Uniformed officers moved through the courthouse, and on some days she found herself avoiding looking too closely at them. When hearings ran late and the building grew quiet and shadowed, she became increasingly uncomfortable with the darkened corridors and empty rooms. She learned to keep moving, to stay surrounded by light and activity, and to prepare herself for the possibility that an unexpected sight or taste or sound could send her mind back to the war. Although she continued functioning at a high level, the effort of holding herself together and keeping the past out of view became increasingly exhausting. Her divorce had already left her living alone, and the sense of isolation she felt inside was sharpened by the belief that no one around her could truly understand what she carried.

What finally brought Marisol to seek help was the growing burden of these experiences as they continued to intrude on her work and private life. She was increasingly troubled by the moments when a memory arrived with full sensory force, the same terror she had once felt overtaking her without warning. She wanted relief from the feeling that the world was dangerous and from the conviction that she had to keep everything hidden to remain acceptable and composed. At intake, she said she did not want to lose control in court or spend the rest of her life arranging herself around reminders of what happened. More than anything, she hoped to be able to move through her days without scanning for uniforms, without dreading anniversaries or darkness, and without feeling as though the event could be seen on her face by everyone around her.
